title: A review of the latest developments regarding the heat treatment effects on hardness, impact toughness, and microstructure in AISI 1040, 4140, and 4340 medium carbon structural steels
abstract: Abstract This review compiles and compares recent research on the influence of various heat treatments on the hardness, impact toughness, and microstructural evolution of AISI 1040, 4140, and 4340 medium carbon structural steels. These steels vary in alloy composition - AISI 1040 is a plain carbon steel, AISI 4140 is Cr-Mo steel, and AISI 4340 is Ni-Cr-Mo alloy steel. For consistent comparison, hardness and impact toughness values reported in the literature were standardized to Rockwell C (HRC) and Charpy impact energy (J). It was observed that due to formation of a ferrite – pearlite structure, annealing produced the softest steels (~ 20 HRC, > 120 J). Normalizing refined pearlite grains and balanced the properties (26–37 HRC, ~ 140 J). Quenching, because of martensite formation, yielded highest hardness (59–70 HRC) but lowest toughness (~ 35 J), while tempering improved toughness (80–150 J) while maintaining a moderate hardness. Heat treatments such as austempering, up-quench austempering (UQA), ultra-fast heat treatment (UFH), laser heat treatment (LHT), deep cryogenic treatment (DCT) and shallow cryogenic treatment (SCT), improved performance by altering mechanical properties through bainitic transformation, carbide precipitation, and surface hardening. Overall, the findings highlight that the hardness-to-toughness relationship varies significantly with the selected heat treatment, underscoring the critical role of tailored heat treatment processes in optimizing the mechanical performance of these steels.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: It’s been observed that in structural, automotive, aerospace and defense industries, medium carbon steels such as AISI 1040, AISI 4140, and AISI 4340 are widely used because of their adaptability to heat treatments which result in balanced hardness, impact toughness, fatigue resistance and wear behavior properties [ 1 ,  2 ,  3 ,  4 ,  5 ,  6 – 7 ]. This is because, different heat treatment methods can affect the formation and arrangement of ferrite, pearlite, martensite and bainite phases on the steel structure, and controlling the rate of formation of these phases through proper heat treatments will give us the desired mechanical properties. Thus, it is very important to understand the role and type of heat treatment required to alter the properties of these steels, so as to get the desired properties.

Heat treatments such as annealing, normalizing, quenching and tempering are the most commonly used methods to alter the properties of medium carbon steels. Extensive studies have been carried out on how these heat treatments effect the mechanical properties of these steels [ 8 ,  9 – 10 ] [ 11 ,  12 – 13 ]. Other methods such as laser-based heat treatment and ultra sonic impact treatment [ 14 ,  15 ,  16 – 17 ], boriding [ 18 ] and cryogenic treatments [ 19 ], are also used to alter the mechanical performance of the steels.

Hybrid methods such as quench-tempering [ 20 ], double quench tempering [ 10 ], austempering [ 21 ], have given varying toughness and hardness combinations for each steel. Even the effects of surface modification methods like turn assisted deep cold rolling [ 22 ], machining induced transformations [ 23 ,  24 ] have been widely researched. Surface hardening treatments and cryogenic treatments [ 25 ], have also been researched. Modern experimental investigative methods such as Barkhausen noise and hysteresis loop techniques, ultra sonic velocity measurements and magnetic nondestructive techniques [ 26 ,  27 – 28 ], have been instrumental in studying the effects of various heat treatments on properties of medium carbon steels, to get a more accurate picture.

In this review we have attempted to understand effects of the various heat treatment methods, both conventional and advanced, used in industry, on the hardness, impact toughness and microstructure of medium carbon structural steels such as AISI 1040, AISI 4140 and AISI 4340, by creating comparison data tables, highlighting industrial implications and identify gaps for future optimization of these steels. For the ease of review, all the hardness data collected from the respective research papers have been standardized and presented in Rockwell C (HRC) scale, and impact toughness has been presented in terms of Charpy impact energy (J). Tables  1 ,  2 , and  3  list all the different types of conventional and advanced heat treatment methods along with modern investigative methods that have been used to study the properties of the respective steels.

Table 1 Conventional heat treatment methods Method Description Annealing [ 13 ], [ 29 ,  30 ,  31 ,  32 ,  33 ,  34 – 35 ] This heat treatment method involves heating the material above its upper-critical temperature for a set time and cooling it slowly in the furnace Normalizing [ 36 ,  1 ,  3 ], [ 37 ,  38 ,  39 ,  40 ,  41 – 42 ] In this method of heat treatment, the material is heated to a state above its critical range temperature, held there for a sufficient amount of time, and then air cooled under atmospheric conditions outside the furnace Hardening/Quenching [ 10 ], [ 43 ,  44 ,  45 ,  46 – 47 ] In this method of heat treatment, the material is heated to a state above its upper critical temperature range, held there for a sufficient amount of time and then quickly cooled through a process called quenching, wherein the heated material is dipped in a liquid cooling medium Tempering [ 10 ], [ 47 ,  48 – 49 ] The hardened/heat treated steel is again reheated to a specific temperature below its critical point and then cooled, which leads to reduced brittleness and increased toughness and ductility Quench & temper [ 10 ] The steel is first heat treated at a temperature above austenitizing temperature and quenched, and then it is again reheated to a specific temperature below critical point and then cooled. This results in a balanced hardness and toughness Asutempering [ 21 ,  34 ,  50 ] In this type of heat treatment, the steel is first heat treated to a temperature above austenitizing temperature, and then rapidly cooled in a medium held at 230 to 400 °C, and then held at that constant temperature to allow isothermal transformation. This results in the formation of pure bainite structure, which improves hardness while maintaining the impact toughness Double quench tempering [ 10 ] This method consists of two stages of quenching and tempering

Table 2 Advanced heat treatment methods Method Description Intercritical dual phase heat treatments [ 51 ,  52 ] In this method of heat treatment, pre heat treated steels are subjected to a different heat treatment at an intercritical temperature. This gives the steel duplex structure Laser hardening [ 14 ,  15 ,  17 ] This method uses high intensity lasers to heat the steel. This results in improved wear and corrosion resistance Boriding [ 18 ] This process involves diffusion of boron atoms into the lattice of the steel surface, which results in improved hardness Ultrasonic impact treatment [ 14 ] This is a high frequency weld impact treatment that improves fatigue resistance of welded structures Tomita heat treatment [ 53 ] This is a new method of up quenching and austempering, to get a fine bainite morphology Ultra-fast heat treatment (UFH) [ 54 ] In this type of heat treatment, the ultrafast heating is done by passing a high intensity current through the steel material, which heats up the material rapidly, and then rapidly cooled within a matter of seconds Eco friendly emulsion quenching [ 9 ] Instead of oil or water, other more eco-friendly emulsions like vegetable oil, brine, egg-yolk emulsions, are used as quenchants Cryogenic treatments [ 25 ], [ 55 ,  56 ,  57 ,  58 ,  59 ,  60 ,  61 ,  62 – 63 ] In this type of treatment, steel is cooled below − 150 °C, typically to − 196 °C, after hardening. The process converts austenite to martensite and precipitates fine carbide during tempering. This improves grain structure, hardness, wear resistance, dimensional stability, and fatigue life without distortion.

Table 3 Modern investigation techniques Methods Description Magnetic Barkhausen noise nondestructive testing (NDE) [ 26 ,  27 ] It is a nondestructive method of analysis wherein the measurement is carried out by analyzing a noise like signal induced in a ferromagnetic material, placed in a magnetic field

A structured literature review process based on transparency guidelines similar to PRISMA was used in this review. Articles were selected from Google Scholar, Scopus, ScienceDirect, and SpringerLink. Following terms were used as keywords: microstructure, hardness, impact toughness/energy, heat treatment, and AISI 1040, 4140, and 4340. The search mainly encompassed publications from 2000 to 2025. The respective research papers were chosen only if the respective steels were equivalent to AISI 1040, 4140 and 4340 steels, subjected to specified heat treatments, and the paper provided quantitative hardness (HRC) and impact toughness (J) results. Papers that did not provide data on mechanical properties or that did not have enough microstructural evidence, were not chosen. For the sake of maintaining uniformity in data comparison, hardness values that were originally reported in Vickers (HV) and Brinell (HB) scales were all converted to Rockwell C (HRC) using ASTM E140-12b [ 63 ] standard conversion relationships. Impact energy values were standardized to Joules (J) following ASTM E23 [ 64 ] guidelines. When studies presented multiple conversion bases, cross-verification was performed using averaged conversion ratios to minimize bias. These standardized units ensured direct comparability among datasets compiled from different research works.

Among the reviewed studies, slight variations in steel alloy composition, heat treatment temperature, and hardness or impact specimen geometry, contributed to differences in reported hardness and toughness values. For the sake of maintaining methodological consistency, only studies adhering to standard alloy composition ranges of AISI 1040, 4140, and 4340 steels, as per ASTM A576-90b [ 65 ], and mechanical characteristics testing within room temperature range, were considered. Wherever multiple data points existed, values were represented as mean.

The carbon content and alloying additions of AISI 1040, 4140, and 4340 steels strongly govern the influence of heat treatment on the microstructures of these steels. Annealing of plain carbon AISI 1040 steel results in a coarse ferrite-pearlite microstructure, with low hardness and excellent ductility [ 33 ], whereas normalizing tends to refine the pearlite and increases toughness and strength [ 37 ]. Although quenching produces a martensitic structure, the thin sections of a material are the only ones that can form martensite due to 1040’s limited hardenability [ 37 ]. Tempered martensite, the result of further tempering, strikes a good mix between toughness and strength, though it only hardens to a moderate depth [ 66 ].

On the other hand, chromium and molybdenum alloyed AISI 4140 steel is more resistant to transformation and hardens more quickly. Structures resembling 1040, but with finer and more homogeneous ferrite-pearlite grains, are produced by annealing and normalizing the material [ 68 ]. The combination of quenching and tempering results in a martensitic structure that is predominant even in thicker cross-sections. Tempered martensite, which contains fine alloy carbides, is extremely tough, resistant to wear, and strong [ 12 ].

The hardenability of the three grades is highest in AISI 4340 steel, which contains nickel along with chromium and molybdenum. In contrast to quenching, which creates uniformly martensitic microstructures across wide areas, tempering produces tempered martensite with alloy carbides dispersed finely, and annealing and normalizing produce ferrite-pearlite structures [ 3 ]. Chromium and molybdenum stabilize carbides, and nickel adds toughness, allowing 4340 to achieve a superior strength-toughness synergy. Hardenability, microstructure refinement, and property tailoring through heat treatment, all increase steadily from 1040 to 4340 steels.

Studies by Fuat Kara and collaborators at Düzce University, have provided a detailed insight into the effects of cryogenic treatment on microstructures of hardened steels. Deep cryogenic treatment refined the steel microstructure by transforming retained austenite into martensite and promoting fine carbide precipitation. Kara et al. [ 60 ,  62 ] and Altan Özbek [ 61 ] reported that holding steels such as Sleipner and 41Cr4 at − 180 °C for 24–36 h, produced dense and uniformly distributed carbides, thus reducing residual austenite by about 36%, and lowering residual stress by nearly 50%. Finer martensite laths, homogeneous carbide dispersion, and stable grain boundaries were observed through XRD, SEM, and EDS analyses.

sections.heading: Effect of heat treatments on hardness and impact toughness of AISI 1040 steel
paragraphs: AISI 1040 steel is a medium carbon structural steel that is widely used in gears, shafts, axles and machine parts. It is a plain carbon steel, where in carbon (0.4%) is the major alloying element. Other elements are present in small negligible quantity. Table  5  presents the alloy composition of AISI 1040 steel as per SAE ASTM A 576-90b [ 65 ] standards and its hardness and impact toughness.
Table 5 AISI 1040 steel composition and properties Element C Si Mn P S Fe Wt % 0.36–0.45 0.10–0.40 0.60–1.60 < 0.050 < 0.050 ~ 98.3 Properties Hardness (HRC) Impact toughness Values 20 20 J

Amongst the conventional heat treatment methods used to alter the properties of AISI 1040 steel, it was observed that annealing led to the formation of a coarse ferrite-pearlite structure, which resulted in a decline in hardness while improving impact toughness. Based on studies by Singh et al., [ 69 ] and Hernandez-Duran et al., [ 33 ], the hardness values for annealed AISI 1040 steel usually vary in the range of 18–22 HRC, while impact toughness falls in the range of 120–190 J. Annealed specimens also exhibit superior corrosion resistance, compared to other heat treatment methods.

Normalizing on the other hand led to the formation of a refined pearlite grain structure, that exhibited an improved hardness ranging from 26 to 37 HRC, while maintaining a moderate toughness of 70–160 J [ 37 ,  70 ]. Fatigue studies by Mossaab et al., [ 71 ], show that normalized C45 medium carbon steels achieved a better life span of ~ 2.8 × 10 6  cycles, compared to ~ 8.4 × 10 5  cycles for quenching. Thus normalized AISI 1040 steel exhibit a balance in hardness and toughness, making them a reliable choice for applications like shafts and axles, where the material is subjected to cyclic loads.

Quenching, which has a higher cooling rate then annealing or normalizing, results in the formation of a martensitic structure that leads to a greater increase in hardness but due to rapid cooling, uneven contractions occur, which results in internal stresses that make the material more brittle. Water quenching achieved the highest hardness values ranging from 59 to 82 HRC, with impact toughness values ranging from 30 to 40 J [ 28 ,  37 ,  52 ,  66 ,  72 ], while oil quenching, which has a comparatively slower cooling rate, produces lower hardness ranging from 45 to 58 HRC, but exhibits better toughness than water quenching [ 41 ]. Even though both types of quenching exhibit higher hardness, the corrosion resistance is lower than that of annealed AISI 1040 steels [ 7 ]. Due to this tempering becomes highly necessary after quenching, because tempering results in the formation of a martensite-bainite structure, wherein precipitation of carbides occur, which result in reduced lattice stresses, thus improving the ductility of the quenched steel. Due to tempering the hardness of AISI 1040 steel decreases to a range of 19–45 HRC, when compared to only quenching, but the toughness increases to a moderate range of 80–150 J, depending on the temperature of heat treatment [ 66 ,  69 ,  73 ]. This balance in hardness and toughness makes quenching followed by tempering the most widely used method of heat treatment for AISI 1040 steel in the industry.

More modern methods of heat treatment such as intercritical heat treatments, laser hardening (LHT), ultrasonic impact treatment (UIT), and ultra-fast heating (UFH) for property altercation of AISI 1040 steel, have also been researched. Study by Gurumurthy et al. [ 52 ], showed that normalized AISI 1040 steel samples that were reheated to varying intercritical temperatures followed by isothermal holding and then air cooled, developed dual phase (ferrite + bainite) structures, that had higher hardness (30 to 48 HRC), but lower impact energy (15 to 20 J) than the normalized samples (28 HRC, 22 J). Similarly, when the steel was subjected to intercritical heat treatment followed by quenching [ 52 ], a ferrite + martensite dual phase structure was obtained that exhibited a considerably higher hardness (42 to 54 HRC) but lower impact energy (5 to 24 J) when compared to the normalized samples (28 HRC, 57 J). Lesyk et al. [ 14 ], showed that laser hardening combined with ultrasonic impact treatment (LHT + UIT), raised the surface hardness of the specimen to a range of 56 to 62 HRC, with a considerable improvement in surface finish. Newer methods of heat treatment such as ultra-fast heat treatment, where the steel is rapidly heated, to temperatures below 100 °C, and then cooled within a matter of 5 to 10 s, was researched by Gaggiotti et al. [ 54 ], exhibited nearly a 10% increase in hrdness, as compared to conventional heat treatment.

Table  6  provides a quantitative summary of the effect of these heat treatments on hardness and impact toughness of AISI 1040 steel, while Fig.  1  presents a pictorial representation of the balance in hardness and impact toughness obtained for different heat treatments for AISI 1040 steel.

sections.heading: Effect of heat treatments on hardness and impact toughness AISI 4140 steels
paragraphs: AISI 4140, a medium carbon alloy steel, with chromium (Cr) and molybdenum (Mo) as the major alloying elements, is widely used for structural applications in automotive and aerospace industry. Table  7  presents the alloy composition of AISI 4140 steel as per SAE ASTM A 576-90b standards [ 65 ] and its hardness and impact toughness.

Table 7 AISI 4140 steel composition and properties Element C Si Mn P S Cr Mo Fe Wt % 0.36–0.45 0.15–0.30 0.50–0.80 < 0.035 < 0.040 0.90–1.50 0.20–0.40 ~ 97 Properties Hardness (HRC) Impact toughness (J) Values 27 25

According to study by Bhagyalaxmi et al. [ 68 ], where the hardness of the as bought AISI 4140 steel was around 21 HRC, observed that heat treating the steel to 900 °C and then subjecting it to annealing lowered the hardness of the steel substantially (10 HRC) while improving ductility, because of the formation of pearlite ferrite structure. Whereas normalizing gave a better combination of ductility and hardness 27 HRC. Hardening treatment gave the highest hardness of 45 HRC but with low ductility and high brittleness. Sharma et al. [ 36 ], who carried out normalizing, austempering and intercritical dual phase heat treatments (ferrite + martensite) on AISI 4140 steel samples, observed that austempering gave the best combination of hardness and impact toughness, with nearly 60% increse in hardness and nearly 20 J increase in impact toughness. While normalizing gave a good combination of hardness and impact energy (21 HRC and 36 J), the dual phase heat treated samples exhibited lower impact toughness (20 J).

Mahmood et al. [ 38 ], who studied the effect of air flow rate on the cooling effect and hardness of AISI 4140 steel subjected to normalizing, concluded that with increase in air flow rate, from 11 to 17 m 3 /s, there was an average increase of 12% i hardness. This clearly showed that, even though the heat treatment involved was normalizing, with increase in cooling rate hardness increased. Thus, quenching heat treatment, which has a higher cooling rate, of AISI 4140 steel, increases its hardness by a lot, as compared to other conventional heat treatments. Basori et al. [ 43 ], reported that, when AISI 4140 steel was subjected to oil quenching at heat treatment temperature of 850 °C, for holding times of 30, 60 and 90 min respectively, the hardness increased with increase in holding time. While time and temperature are important factors that affect hardness and impact toughness of AISI 4140 steel, the quenching media and its respective cooling rate is also a very important factor that influences hardness especially. Chuaiphan et al. [ 11 ], who researched the effect of water quenching, oil quenching, quenching and tempering and normalizing, on AISI 4140 steel, for base cutter cane harvester application, where hardness of the material is of utmost importance, observed that water quenched samples exhibited the highest hardness, around 60 HRC, and the lowest impact toughness of ~ 12 J, while hardness for oil quenched samples was in the range of 25 to 45 HRC, with a slightly better impact toughness of 15 J. Normalizing gave the lowest hardness of ~ 25 HRC, but had the highest impact toughness of ~ 40 J. The quenched and tempered samples exhibited a good balance in hardness and impact toughness. This is because as the cooling rate increases, the quantity of martensitic grain size increases, thus increasing hardness. But impact toughness gets inversely affected, because higher cooling rate leads to formation of lattice stresses that make the quenched steel more brittle. Sharma et al. [ 12 ], also reported that increase in cooling rate had a positive impact on hardness, while impact toughness decreased. They studied the effect of water, ice water, salt water, coconut oil and castor oil on hardness of AISI 4140 steel, and reported that ice water quenching exhibited the highest hardness of 51 HRC, while coconut oil quenching had the lowest hardness of 35 HRC. Bhagya Laxmi et al. [ 74 ], who studied the effect of quenching of AISI 4140 steel in Pinnay oil, viscosity of 41 centistokes, and Karanja oil, viscosity of 30 centistokes, for tempering temperatures of 340 to 490 °C, observed that the lower viscous oil at the lower temperature, exhibited the highest hardness of 46 HRC and lowest impact energy of 28 J. As the viscosity of the quenching media increased the hardness decreased and impact toughness increased, with a similar trend seen for increase in tempering temperature.

sections.heading: Effect of heat treatments on hardness and impact toughness AISI 4340 steels
paragraphs: Precisely controlled heat treatments give 43xx series steels, such as AISI 4340, their hardness and toughness. Because of their wide range of applications in the aeronautics industry, understanding and choosing the right type of heat treatment, to alter the properties of AISI 4340 is essential. It is a nickel-chromium-molybdenum (Ni-Cr-Mo) alloy steel. Table  9  lists the alloy composition of AISI 4340 steel as per SAE ASTM A 576-90b standards [ 65 ] and its hardness and impact toughness.

Table 9 AISI 4340 steel composition and properties Element C Si Mn P S Cr Ni Mo Fe Wt % 0.36–0.45 0.10–0.35 0.45–0.70 < 0.050 < 0.050 0.90–1.40 1.30–1.80 0.20–0.35 ~ 95 Properties Hardness (HRC) Impact toughness (J) Values 29 31

Conventional heat treatments like annealing, normalizing and hardening are extensively used to alter AISI 4340 steel properties. Kandpal et al. [ 3 ], studied the effect of annealing, normalizing and water quenching at 910 °C heating temperature and 30 min holding time, and reported a hardness of 21 HRC for annealing, 34 HRC normalizing and 42 HRC for water quenching. Study conducted by Sharma and Pandey [ 75 ], investigated the effect of normalizing, hardening and tempering on AISI 4340 steel, and found that the hardness of harden tempered steel (49 HRC), was higher than that of normalized samples (39 HRC). Lee and Su [ 20 ], realized that, when AISI 4340 steel was subjected to quenching and progressive tempering from 100 to 650 °C, for holding times of 2 h and 48 h respectively, holding time had a negligible effect, while temperature had the major effect on hardness. As tempering temperature increased from 100 to 650 °C, the hardness gradually decreased from 60 to 36 HRC.

In intercritical dual phase heat treatments conducted by Gurumurthy et al. [ 67 ], even though the water quenched (37 HRC) and austempered (34 HRC) specimens had a considerably higher hardness than the ferrite-bainite (29 HRC) and ferrite-martensite specimens (32 HRC), the ferrite- bainite and austempered specimens had a better balance in hardness and impact toughness.

Certain modern heat treatment methods, such as the Tomita method, has also been employed. The Tomita method is a up quench austempering method where the steel is subjected to heat treatment at a austenitizing temperature, and then quenched in an austempering medium two times, first at a lower temperature and then at a higher temperature, and then air cooled. This results in the formation of a tempered martensite and bainite structure that has better hardness and impact toughness. Safi and Givi [ 53 ], studied the difference in the steels properties when it was subjected to upper bainite austempering, lower bainite austempering and Tomita heat treatments, and found that the Tomita heat treated steel samples exhibited the better combination of hardness (54 HRC) and impact toughness (33 J).

sections.heading: Advanced cryogenic heat treatment methods and their effects on hardened steels
paragraphs: Extensive research has been carried out on effects of cryogenic and EDM assisted treatments on properties of hardened steels. Kara et al. [ 55 ] found that deep cryogenic treatment at −196 °C for 30 h, followed by tempering at 200 °C for 2 h increased surface integrity and reduced surface roughness of AISI 5140 steel subject to cylindrical grinding. This improvement was due to uniform dispersion of fine carbide precipitates, which resulted in lowered grinding temperature and improved hardness and wear resistance. Nas et al. [ 56 ] reported that post heat treatment surface modifications such as cryogenic conditioning with controlled energy input, on AISI D2 steel processed by electroerosion machining, optimized surface finish without compromising on hardness, thus improving the steels surface roughness. Özbek and Özbek [ 57 ] carried out shallow cryogenic treatment of 1.2436 tool steel at − 80 °C for 12 h and 18 h, due to which there was an increase in carbide density by ~ 18.8%, hardness by 9%, and wear resistance by 34%, thus proving that even shallow cryogenic exposure improved hardness–wear synergy through controlled carbide refinement. Özbek and Özbek [ 59 ] and Kara et al. [ 58 ], also reported that deep cryogenic treatments, of X210CrW12 and tool steels, at −180 °C And − 196 °C for longer soaking times, raised hardness by ~ 12%, improved wear resistance by ~ 59%, increased tensile and yield strength by ~ 11%, and improved surface roughness and tool life by 25% and 150% respectively. Similar research by Kara et al. and Altan Özbek [ 61 ,  62 ], reported a raise in hardness by 6 to10%, improvement in wear resistance by up to 60%, and enhanced dimensional stability. Overall, cryogenic treatment homogenizes the microstructure, strengthens the martensitic matrix, and provides a refined, stress-relieved structure responsible for higher hardness and improved fatigue performance in tool and structural steels. These findings correlate with the current review, that precise thermal management after hardening enhances machinability and dimensional stability in steels of comparable hardenability.

sections.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: The data collected from the respective research papers for AISI 10,440, 4140, and 4340 steels, demonstrates how heat treatment is essential for tailoring mechanical properties of the steels to suit for particular needs in the field. Table  11  summarizes the relationship between most commonly used heat treatment methods and their applications, for industrial optimization.

Table 11 Industrial applications of AISI 1040, 4140, and 4340 steels based on heat treatment and property balance Steel type Heat treatment route Key property advantage Recommended industrial applications AISI 1040 Normalizing Balanced strength and toughness Shafts, axles, connecting rods AISI 1040 Quench + Temper Moderate hardness, improved fatigue life Gears, crank pins AISI 4140 Oil Quench + Temper High wear resistance, good ductility Power transmission shafts, spindles AISI 4140 Austempering Enhanced strength–toughness synergy Drive shafts, gear blanks AISI 4340 Quench + Temper (200–650 °C) Wide tunability, excellent strength Aircraft landing gear, heavy-duty fasteners AISI 4340 Tomita/Up-Quench Austempering High strength with improved toughness Dies, turbine shafts, high-stress bolts AISI 4340/4140 Deep Cryogenic Treatment (− 196 °C, 24–36 h) + Temper Refined microstructure, high wear resistance, reduced residual stress Aerospace shafts, dies, injection molds, precision tools, bearings AISI D2/5140 (Reference steels) Cryogenic + EDM/Grinding Optimization Improved surface integrity, reduced roughness, enhanced fatigue life Cutting tools, forming dies, valve components, gear tools

Annealing, normalizing, quenching, and tempering are some of the traditional treatments for plain carbon AISI 1040 steel. These processes produced predictable trade-offs in ductility, toughness, hardness, and fatigue resistance. The usefulness of AISI 1040 in environments with high wear is further enhanced by new techniques like laser hardening (LHT) and ultrasonic fatigue hardening (UFH). Quenching produces a hard martensitic structure, tempering improves ductility, and advanced methods such as double quench tempering, austempering, and intercritical dual phase heat treatments, optimize the strength-toughness balance through processes like grain refinement, bainitic transformation, or carbide precipitation, leading to enhanced tunability in AISI 4140 steel. Higher-alloy AISI 4340 steel offers a wider range of properties after similar treatment processes, which makes it useful for a variety of applications. Cryogenic treatments produced refined microstructure, reducing residual stress that resulted in superior hardness, wear resistance, and dimensional stability, making it an effective post-heat-treatment route for high-strength structural steels. Inadequate statistical validation, a lack of microstructural quantification using advanced techniques (EBSD/TEM), and incomplete datasets on fatigue and impact are some of the persistent deficiencies that these results revealed, while also indicating that treatment pathways determine the final property balance. In order to bridge the gap between lab results and industrial implementation, it is essential to address these shortcomings.

tables.caption: Conventional heat treatment methods
rows: This heat treatment method involves heating the material above its upper-critical temperature for a set time and cooling it slowly in the furnace

In this method of heat treatment, the material is heated to a state above its critical range temperature, held there for a sufficient amount of time, and then air cooled under atmospheric conditions outside the furnace

In this method of heat treatment, the material is heated to a state above its upper critical temperature range, held there for a sufficient amount of time and then quickly cooled through a process called quenching, wherein the heated material is dipped in a liquid cooling medium
The hardened/heat treated steel is again reheated to a specific temperature below its critical point and then cooled, which leads to reduced brittleness and increased toughness and ductility

The steel is first heat treated at a temperature above austenitizing temperature and quenched, and then it is again reheated to a specific temperature below critical point and then cooled. This results in a balanced hardness and toughness

In this type of heat treatment, the steel is first heat treated to a temperature above austenitizing temperature, and then rapidly cooled in a medium held at 230 to 400 °C, and then held at that constant temperature to allow isothermal transformation. This results in the formation of pure bainite structure, which improves hardness while maintaining the impact toughness
This method consists of two stages of quenching and tempering

tables.caption: Advanced heat treatment methods
rows: In this method of heat treatment, pre heat treated steels are subjected to a different heat treatment at an intercritical temperature. This gives the steel duplex structure
This method uses high intensity lasers to heat the steel. This results in improved wear and corrosion resistance
This process involves diffusion of boron atoms into the lattice of the steel surface, which results in improved hardness
This is a high frequency weld impact treatment that improves fatigue resistance of welded structures
This is a new method of up quenching and austempering, to get a fine bainite morphology

In this type of heat treatment, the ultrafast heating is done by passing a high intensity current through the steel material, which heats up the material rapidly, and then rapidly cooled within a matter of seconds
Instead of oil or water, other more eco-friendly emulsions like vegetable oil, brine, egg-yolk emulsions, are used as quenchants

In this type of treatment, steel is cooled below − 150 °C, typically to − 196 °C, after hardening. The process converts austenite to martensite and precipitates fine carbide during tempering. This improves grain structure, hardness, wear resistance, dimensional stability, and fatigue life without distortion.
